name: Optimism Bias
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why the Roadmap Always Says Five More Years
lesson.summary: Optimism bias, the well documented tendency to overestimate favorable outcomes and underestimate timelines and difficulty, helps explain why practical quantum advantage has been described as roughly a decade away for more than two decades running.
lesson.body:
Optimism bias is a genuine, extensively studied cognitive tendency: people systematically overestimate the likelihood of good outcomes and underestimate how long things will take or how hard they will be, and this tendency tends to be strongest, not weakest, among people who are closest to and most personally invested in a project. It is important to separate this from dishonesty. Someone affected by optimism bias is not lying, they genuinely believe the more favorable estimate, which is precisely what makes the bias so persistent and hard to correct for.

The pattern shows up reliably outside quantum computing, which is what makes it useful as a comparison. Software project timelines are a textbook example, studied extensively within software engineering, where initial schedule estimates are systematically shorter than actual delivery times across countless organizations and decades. Large infrastructure megaprojects show a similar pattern, researchers including Bent Flyvbjerg have documented consistent cost and schedule overruns across many countries, project types, and time periods, not as isolated failures but as a recurring statistical regularity. When a pattern shows up this consistently across unrelated domains, it points to something about how humans forecast under uncertainty rather than something specific to any one field.

Quantum computing timelines fit this pattern closely. Claims that practical, broadly useful quantum advantage sits roughly five to ten years in the future have been made by serious, credentialed researchers and well funded companies since at least the early 2000s, and similar claims with a similar time horizon continue to be made today. Unlike, say, artificial intelligence, where benchmark performance visibly and measurably compounds year over year, quantum computing predictions have a harder time pointing to a steadily closing gap between the current state and the promised outcome, which makes the recurrence of the same rough timeframe across two decades worth noticing rather than dismissing.

A useful and somewhat counterintuitive detail about optimism bias is that expertise does not protect against it, and may even amplify it. Deep technical knowledge and genuine passion for a field tend to correlate with strong belief in that field's near-term potential, since people who did not believe in the potential rarely stay in the field long enough to become experts in it. This is worth remembering specifically when a physicist with genuine, hard-won credentials states with confidence that a breakthrough is imminent, expertise establishes that the person understands the technical details, it does not establish that their timeline forecast is unbiased.

Optimism bias also does not operate alone. It compounds naturally with the sunk cost fallacy discussed in the previous chapter: believing a payoff is close makes continued investment feel more clearly justified, which in turn makes it harder to revise the timeline downward later without appearing to have wasted the intervening years, a reinforcing loop that the chapter on compounding biases returns to directly.
